tagline: A lakeshore drive through the country that supplied the Comstock mines
intro: Lake Tahoe’s Eastshore Drive follows Nevada’s shore through a landscape of lake, pines and mountains. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway at 28 miles and allows one hour for the drive, or a few hours to enjoy the route. Its description emphasizes those lake and mountain views. Along SR 28, the road alternates between state park and national forest, with a shoreline stretch of approximately four miles.

The road that became SR 28 served timber flumes from 1880 and was paved around 1932. At Cave Rock, a single-lane bridge built in 1863 carried the Lincoln Highway before the first tunnel bore opened in 1931 to increase road capacity. Nevada designated that highway the North Shore Road scenic byway in 1994. In 1996, SR 28 and part of US 50 together became the nationally designated Eastshore Drive.

Begin at Crystal Bay on the California line and follow SR 28 through Incline Village toward Sand Harbor. Beyond the harbor, the highway passes through forest and parkland to Spooner Junction, just south of Spooner Lake. The US 50 portion continues past Glenbrook and through Cave Rock’s tunnels toward Zephyr Cove. South of Zephyr Cove, US 50 crosses Round Hill Village toward Stateline.

moments.title: Incline Village
moments.text: Incline Village takes its name from a railway built to move timber uphill. The Sierra Nevada Wood and Lumber Company worked on Tahoe’s northeast side, supplying timber for the late nineteenth-century mining boom at the Comstock Lode in Virginia City. Its railway lifted timber 1,400 feet before a gravity flume carried it toward a tunnel to Carson City. The village was established in 1882. SR 28 crosses the community inland from the shoreline before returning to the lake toward Crystal Bay. The industrial name remains attached to a town on Tahoe’s north shore.

moments.title: Sand Harbor
moments.text: Sand Harbor once received trees towed across Tahoe behind the steamship Niagara. By the 1870s, Walter Scott Hobart had established Sierra Nevada Wood & Lumber Company operations here. Logs went by rail to the Incline sawmill; lumber and cordwood continued to the Comstock Mining District by tramway and flumes. The harbor now has gently sloping beaches and rock formations beside clear water. The one-third-mile Sand Point Nature Trail provides interpretive signs along a short walking route. Cedars and Jeffrey pines shade the picnic area, and the Lake Tahoe Shakespeare Festival brings plays here in July and August.
moments.notice: Notice the rock formations beside the gently sloping beaches.

moments.title: Glenbrook
moments.text: Logs reached Glenbrook’s mills by stream and barge from forests near the lake. Augustus W. Pray arrived among settlers in 1860 and built a sawmill the following year. By 1875, the town had four sawmills, two hotels, a store, a bowling alley and a billiard hall. Glenbrook supplied timber to the Comstock Lode and Virginia City, but logging declined after 1880 and ended by the century’s close. Its name came from the former Glenbrook House hotel, itself named for the valley and stream. The lakeside community now has a private beach and bay for residents and renters, with no public access.

practical: Sand Harbor: Day-use reservations are required for vehicle entry from 8 to 10 a.m., May 15 through September 30. Parking or dropping off on Highway 28 outside designated parking is prohibited. (checked 2026-10-11)
